{{Short description|Shape that can be represented as a linear matrix inequality}}
[[File:S asdf rot.png|thumb|A spectrahedron]]

In [[convex geometry]], a '''spectrahedron''' is a shape that can be represented as a [[linear matrix inequality]]. Alternatively, the set of {{math|''n'' &times; ''n''}} [[positive semidefinite matrix|positive semidefinite matrices]] forms a [[convex cone]] in {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n'' &times; ''n''</sup>}}, and a spectrahedron is a shape that can be formed by intersecting this cone with an [[affine subspace]].

Spectrahedra are the [[feasible region|feasible regions]] of [[semidefinite programming|semidefinite programs]].<ref>{{citation|first1=Motakuri|last1=Ramana|first2=A. J.|last2=Goldman|author2-link= Alan J. Goldman |title=Some geometric results in semidefinite programming|journal=Journal of Global Optimization|volume=7|issue=1|pages=33–50|year=1995|doi=10.1007/BF01100204}}.</ref> The images of spectrahedra under [[Affine transformation|linear or affine transformations]] are called ''projected spectrahedra'' or ''spectrahedral shadows''. Every spectrahedral shadow is a [[convex set]] that is also [[Semialgebraic set|semialgebraic]], but the converse (conjectured to be true until 2017) is false.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Scheiderer|first=C.|date=2018-01-01|title=Spectrahedral Shadows|journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Algebra and Geometry|volume=2|pages=26–44|doi=10.1137/17m1118981|doi-access=free}}</ref>

An example of a spectrahedron is the '''spectraplex''', defined as

: <math>\mathrm{Spect}_n = \{ X \in \mathbf{S}^n_+ \mid \operatorname{Tr}(X) = 1\}</math>,

where <math>\mathbf{S}^n_+</math> is the set of {{math|''n'' &times; ''n''}} positive semidefinite matrices and <math>\operatorname{Tr}(X)</math> is the [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of the matrix <math>X</math>.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Approximation Algorithms and Semidefinite Programming|url=https://archive.org/details/approximationalg00grtn_585|url-access=limited|last=Gärtner|first=Bernd|last2=Matousek|first2=Jiri|publisher=Springer Science and Business Media|year=2012|isbn=978-3-642-22015-9|pages=[https://archive.org/details/approximationalg00grtn_585/page/n88 76]}}</ref> The spectraplex is a compact set, and can be thought of as the "semidefinite" analog of the [[simplex]].
